title: Floyd State Cycle Detection: Mental Model

answers: Its invariant and the state changed by one step
A recursive implementation in every case
writing.exampleCaption: Rust sketch · target O(mu + lambda) time · O(1) space
writing.explanation:
Begin with the concrete question: Given next indexes, return the first value in the cycle reached from index 0. For the visible input `next=[1,2,3,1]`, the stated result is `1`. Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. A scan turns a sequence into a small piece of state. Say what the state means after the first i elements, before you describe a loop body. That is the mental model for Floyd State Cycle Detection; it gives you a reason for each update instead of a line of code to memorise.

The core mechanism is this: Advance one state once and another twice; their meeting proves a cycle without a visited set. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true. If an item is skipped, inserted, or removed, explain why that action cannot destroy an answer that should be retained. A useful trace has columns for the current input position, the state before the step, the action, and the state afterward. Use the visible sample until the expected result becomes inevitable rather than merely plausible.

Now inspect the Rust sketch, not just its final expression. The supplied Rust sketch is a starting point. Identify what it stores, how one iteration changes it, and whether it already solves the exact task or only demonstrates a related operation. A borrowed slice and a for loop usually express the traversal clearly; distinguish an index you need to return from a value you merely read. Translate the variable names into roles: input, carried state, temporary candidate, and output. Borrow data that only needs reading; copy or move data only when the algorithm actually needs ownership. If the sketch leaves out parsing or edge handling, list those missing steps before calling it a complete solution.

Finally justify the stated bound, O(mu + lambda) time · O(1) space. Count how often an item, edge, state, or candidate can enter the main operation; do not infer the bound from the number of loop keywords alone. Use an empty slice and a one-element slice as checks. Initial values must not silently assume that at least one item exists. Predict the result for a smallest legal input and for one case that stresses the invariant. If your prediction disagrees with a hand trace, repair the state definition before changing code.
writing.feedback: The invariant explains both correctness and which state may change.
writing.question: What should you identify before translating this pattern into Rust?
writing.rule: Preserve the invariant first; the implementation is a consequence of it.
writing.success: You can explain the invariant, termination condition, and O(mu + lambda) time · O(1) space bound without looking at the code.
